questions.q: What is the central ambiguity this lesson says every integration timeout or dropped connection creates for the caller?
options: Whether the network connection used TCP or UDP
Whether the request was never received, failed before completing, or completed but the response was lost — three situations that look identical to the caller but call for different reactions
Whether the remote system is hosted on-premises or in the cloud
Whether the caller used REST or SOAP to make the request
questions.explain: A timeout looks the same to the caller whether the request never arrived, failed mid-processing, or actually succeeded with the response lost in transit — and only one of those three outcomes makes a retry safe, which is exactly the ambiguity idempotency is designed to resolve.

questions.q: Which operation is naturally idempotent, per this lesson's examples?
options: Incrementing a counter by one
Creating a brand-new record every time the operation runs
Setting a record's Status field to a fixed value such as "Shipped"
Appending a new line item to a growing list
questions.explain: Setting a field to a fixed value is naturally idempotent — running it twice leaves the record in exactly the same state as running it once. Incrementing a counter or creating a new record each time are naturally non-idempotent, since repeating them changes the result.

questions.q: How does an idempotency key solve the duplicate-operation problem for an operation that isn't naturally idempotent?
options: It encrypts the request so it can only be processed once, after which the key self-destructs
It uniquely identifies a specific business operation; the receiving system checks whether that key was already processed and, if so, returns the prior result instead of repeating the underlying work
It guarantees the network will never time out again for that specific request
It converts a non-idempotent operation into a batch job automatically
questions.explain: An idempotency key lets the receiving system recognize a retried request as a duplicate of a specific business action it already handled, returning the original result instead of performing the operation (such as creating an order) a second time.

questions.q: Per this lesson, should an idempotency key be generated per individual HTTP attempt or per logical business operation?
options: Per individual HTTP attempt, so each retry gets its own unique key
Per logical business operation, so every retry of the same underlying action (such as the same order) reuses the same key
It doesn't matter which, since the receiving system ignores the key value entirely
A new random key should be generated by the receiving system, not the caller
questions.explain: The key represents the business action being attempted (for example, a specific order), not the individual network attempt — every retry of that same order must send the same key so the receiving system can recognize it as a duplicate of the same operation.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend when an operation genuinely cannot be made idempotent (for example, an irreversible call to a legacy system with no way to check prior execution)?
options: Always retry automatically regardless of risk, since idempotency is unnecessary for rare edge cases
Abandon the integration entirely, since non-idempotent operations can never be integrated safely

Either add a processed-keys lookup to the remote system, accept the risk with a human review step instead of automatic retry, or redesign the interaction so the risky step follows a safely-retryable confirmation step
Convert the operation to use the Bulk API, which is immune to idempotency concerns
questions.explain: When true idempotency isn't achievable, the architect's realistic options are investing in a way for the remote system to detect duplicates, accepting the risk and routing to human review instead of automatic retry, or restructuring the flow so the irreversible step only happens after a safely-retryable confirmation.
